journal.title: How a kantha is made
journal.metaDescription: From layering old saris to the last running stitch: the four stages of making a kantha throw, and why it takes weeks.
body: A kantha starts with cloth that already has a life. Stitchers collect old cotton saris, wash them and lay three or four on top of each other.
The layers are tacked together along the edges, then the stitcher draws the main motif lightly in chalk. Most of the pattern is not drawn at all; it grows from the rows of stitches.
The running stitch is small and even, about six stitches to the inch. A full throw has tens of thousands of them, which is why one person takes two to four weeks.
Last, the throw is washed again. The cotton shrinks a little around the thread and the surface gets its soft, rippled texture.

journal.title: Caring for hand-stitched cotton
journal.metaDescription: Kantha is tougher than it looks. Cold water, a gentle cycle and a line to dry on are all it needs. Skip the dryer.
body: Kantha is tougher than it looks. Cold water, a gentle cycle and a line to dry on are all it needs.
Skip the dryer. Heat can tighten the cotton unevenly and pucker the stitches.
If a stitch catches, do not pull it. Push the loop back through to the reverse side with a blunt needle.
